equivalent: No build found tells it apart from the rules, so it is counted as equivalent, not as a failure. Only a square locks to a tile it does not rest on (a level square beside it), so only such a square can join a group through a lock alone. If it is not also seated squarely on a tile, the group gains the square and the square's own contacts (all outside the group), which reach its middle; the group was balanced, so its centre and the square's middle both lie within the new support, and so does the centre of both: the group stays balanced, and skipping it changes nothing. When the square is also seated squarely on a tile of another piece, no proof is known, but 15,000 random games of up to 20 tiles played with the rules and this mutant side by side found no drop where they differ, nor does the enumeration to depth 6 (tier 1's mutant run). A further 4,000 random games of up to 40 tiles on half 1, 2 and 3 (4.9 million drops, squares favoured, half the games preferring squares locked beside a square) found none either, nor did conformance round 2's beam searches steered to exactly that case (769,000 drops on half 2 and 3 with the rules and this mutant side by side; 168,353 groups the mutant skips, none of them unbalanced, the least slack 0.056 tiles). Conformance round 3 sharpened the open case: a skipped group can change only if the square also merges a piece whose old group is not inside the skipped one (otherwise the group only gains the square, whose own contacts reach its middle); beam searches steered to exactly such groups compared rules.js and this mutant on 3.49 million drops on half 2 to 5 and reached 1,860 drops where such a skipped group does tip (half 4), but each time a lower failing piece that the mutant tests too was reported, so no output differed. If a build ever kills it, it is reported KILLED.
